basic_information.short_title: General Appropriations Act of the Bangsamoro, FY 2024
basic_information.official_title: AN ACT APPROPRIATING FUNDS FOR THE OPERATION OF THE BANGSAMORO GOVERNMENT FROM JANUARY ONE TO DECEMBER THIRTY-ONE, TWO THOUSAND AND TWENTY-FOUR AND FOR OTHER PURPOSES

citizen_summary.what_is_this_about: The region's ₱98.47 billion budget for 2024 — the first Bangsamoro budget written to run for 2 years instead of 1, which ended the annual ritual of passing a separate act to extend the last one.
citizen_summary.why_was_it_proposed: The Bangsamoro Government requires an annual appropriations act to operate. This one covers 1 January to 31 December 2024 and was published under the theme “Accelerating Structural Reforms, Boosting Sustainable Development, and Enhancing Human Capital in the Bangsamoro”.
citizen_summary.what_will_change: ₱98,467,200,000.00 is appropriated from the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges. The act funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 6 special purpose funds, and carries 72 sections of general provisions.
who_will_be_affected: Everyone in the region, through the ministries and services this funds
Constituent local government units, through a ₱6.54 billion support fund and a ₱2.03 billion tax share
All Bangsamoro Government personnel, whose allowances and bonuses it raises
Contractors and suppliers, through procurement and disclosure rules
Personnel who had been receiving hazard duty pay, which this act drops

what_this_means_for_you.in_short: This is a money law: it decides how much funding BARMM ministries and programs get - the schools, hospitals, roads, scholarships, and social services you use are all paid from it. No single citizen 'applies' for it, but nearly every public service you touch depends on it.
in_practice: Sets each ministry's budget ceiling for the year (or adds/extends funds mid-year for supplementals and extensions)
Slow disbursement is the recurring issue - several BAAs exist purely to extend the validity of unspent funds
Big-ticket items to watch: education (MBHTE), health (MOH), public works (MPW), and the Special Development Fund for conflict-affected communities

for_specific_groups.Parents & students: Classroom construction, teacher hiring, and scholarship slots are set here
for_specific_groups.Patients: Hospital operating budgets, medicines, and health worker salaries flow from this law
for_specific_groups.Workers & suppliers: Government projects and procurement opportunities follow the appropriations
for_specific_groups.Taxpayers: This is the accountability document - compare what was appropriated with what was actually delivered

watch_out_for: A law appropriating funds is a promise on paper: actual services depend on the budget being released and spent - ask the implementing ministry for the implementation timeline.
Follow-up reports: the Parliament itself has passed resolutions demanding ministries account for these funds
what_this_means_for_you.when_you_will_feel_it: Laws take effect shortly after publication, but felt impact follows budgets, IRRs, and agency rollout - typically months, not days
what_you_can_do: Ask your municipal/barangay office or the implementing ministry how and when it will roll out where you live
Read the full text (PDF) on the Parliament's website or the Official Gazette of the Bangsamoro - the final sections say when it takes effect and who must act
If it isn't being implemented, raise it with your Member of Parliament or through the ministry's public assistance desk

key_terms_explained.BAA: Bangsamoro Autonomy Act - a regional law passed by the Bangsamoro Parliament, applying inside BARMM alongside national laws.
key_terms_explained.IRR: Implementing Rules and Regulations - the ministry-issued 'how-to' that turns a law's text into procedures; many laws only bite once the IRR is out.
key_terms_explained.GAA: General Appropriations Act - the annual budget law deciding how much each ministry and program gets.

benefits.headline: Funds every public service you use - the enabler of all other benefits.

direct_benefits.benefit: Operating budgets for schools, hospitals, roads, scholarships, social programs
Salaries of teachers, health workers, and government personnel
Special Development Fund projects in conflict-affected communities

indirect_benefits: Procurement and job opportunities from funded projects
Predictability: agencies can plan the year
limitations: Benefits arrive only as fast as funds are released and the implementing office organizes - expect a lag between enactment and service.
Compare appropriations vs. actual delivery - Parliament's own resolutions demand these reports; you can too

key_provisions: Section 1 — Appropriation of Funds. ₱98,467,200,000.00 is appropriated “out of the annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, share in the National Government taxes, fees and charges collected in the Bangsamoro territorial jurisdiction, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges” for the operation of the Bangsamoro Government from 1 January to 31 December 2024. The published volume carries the theme “Accelerating Structural Reforms, Boosting Sustainable Development, and Enhancing Human Capital in the Bangsamoro”, with the initials A, B and E set out as an acronym on the cover.

Bangsamoro Government Budget — The act funds 17 ministries and 11 other executive offices. It is the first to use the term “Ministries, Offices, and Agencies” throughout the general provisions. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority receives ₱4,831,206,302.00, or 4.9% of the total: General Administration and Support ₱760,262,188, Support to Operations ₱472,166,974 and Operations ₱3,598,777,140. Within Operations the act sets a Legislation programme of ₱1,499,577,140 (Personnel Services ₱1,176,937,140, MOOE ₱314,640,000, Capital Outlays ₱8,000,000), Representations/Constituency Building ₱1,654,656,000, Oversight ₱384,544,000, a Parliamentary Learning Program ₱40,000,000 and a Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum ₱20,000,000.

Special purpose funds — 6 funds, up from 5. The Pension and Gratuity Fund is ₱416,115,167.00, the Miscellaneous Personnel Benefit Fund ₱3,408,608,644.00 and the Contingent Fund ₱3,775,038,731.00 — down from ₱5.03 billion the year before, and still carrying the “provision for cost of acquisition of Al-Amanah Islamic Bank and other related costs” alongside a Transitional Development Impact Fund. The Special Development Fund holds at ₱5,000,000,000.00. The Local Government Support Fund rises to ₱6,536,000,000.00, nearly 3 times its FY 2023 level, and a new line appears: the Share of the Constituent Local Government Units in Taxes within the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region, at ₱2,033,183,600.00.

Sections 2–14 (Receipts and Income) — The act itself serves as the allotment order except for appropriations with pre-release conditions and lump sums without release details. Fees, charges and revenues are remitted to the Bangsamoro Treasury under Book VII of BAA 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code, and form part of the general fund, with the schedule of fees posted on agency websites and displayed prominently in every provincial, municipal and field office. Foreign grants require prior clearance from the President. Trust receipts, performance bonds, public-private partnership receipts and revolving funds are separately regulated, with revolving funds barred from paying discretionary and representation expenses. Section 10 requires the Treasury to publish, on the finance ministry's website, the agency, funding source, legal basis and allowable uses of every Special Account and Fund. National internal revenue taxes and import duties on foreign donations, grants and loans are deemed automatically appropriated.

Sections 15–24 (Expenditure) — Procurement follows existing government procurement law, with early procurement authorised up to award and common-use supplies bought from the Procurement Service. Supply inventories are capped at a 3-month requirement. Infrastructure projects may not be sited in critical geohazard areas or no-build zones, must meet the structural strength and climate resilience standards set by the Ministry of Public Works, and must minimise biodiversity loss within the National Integrated Protected Area System; engineering and administrative overhead is capped at 1% of project funds for projects costing more than ₱1,000,000. Rainwater collection systems are required in public markets, school sites and government buildings. A Certification of Availability of Funds is required before any obligation, and a Multi-Year Contractual Authority before any multi-year contract.

Sections 25–33 (Cross-cutting programmes) — Every ministry, office and agency must formulate a Gender and Development Plan integrated into its regular activities amounting to at least 5% of its budget, following RA 9710, the Magna Carta of Women. Agencies must address senior citizens and persons with disability, and all government infrastructure must include accessibility features. Section 28 continues the direction to mainstream Islamic or Shari'ah-compliant finance, with the Chief Minister to promulgate guidelines on the recommendation of the Technical Working Group on Islamic Finance. Built heritage and cultural landscapes may be altered only with the Chief Minister's prior approval. Disaster risk reduction and climate change adaptation must be built into projects, energy efficiency measures adopted, biodiversity protected, and structures in seismically vulnerable areas repaired and retrofitted.

Sections 34–48 (Personnel benefits) — Section 34 caps Personnel Services for one fiscal year at 45% of the Bangsamoro Government's total revenue sources, under Section 6, Article XII of RA 11054. Section 36 sets annual extraordinary expenses at ₱264,000 for the Chief Minister, ₱108,000 for each Deputy Chief Minister, the Speaker and each Member of the Parliament, ₱45,600 for each Minister and ₱26,400 for each Deputy Minister or Bangsamoro Director-General. Section 40 provides that deductions may never reduce an employee's monthly net take-home pay below ₱5,000 — unchanged since FY 2020. Section 41 grants PERA of ₱2,000 a month, also unchanged since FY 2020. Section 42 raises the uniform or clothing allowance to ₱7,000 a year, from ₱6,000. Section 45 raises monthly representation and transportation allowances to ₱15,500 for the Chief Minister, ₱12,500 for Deputy Chief Ministers, the Speaker and Members of the Parliament, ₱10,000 for Ministers, ₱9,500 for Deputy Ministers, ₱8,500 for Director II and Director III and ₱6,000 for Chiefs of Division and Director I — the first increase since FY 2020. Sections 46 and 47 grant a mid-year bonus of 1 month's basic salary and a year-end bonus of 1 month plus a ₱5,000 cash gift. Hazard duty pay, carried in every budget from FY 2020 through FY 2023, does not appear in this act.

Sections 49–62 (Release and use of funds) — Section 49 is the structural change. Appropriations are available for release and obligation until 31 December 2025 — 2 years rather than 1 — except Personnel Services and General Administration and Support MOOE, valid for obligation until 31 December 2024 only. Appropriations obligated as of 31 December 2025 for the completion, inspection and payment of Capital Outlays, and for the delivery, inspection and payment of MOOE under Support to Operations and Operations, “shall be valid until fully expended”. The constituent LGUs' shares in national taxes collected in the region and the local government support fund “shall be available until fully released, obligated, and disbursed” — they do not lapse at all. Funds transferred between organisational units, between agencies or to local government units are not considered disbursed until actually used to pay for completed construction, goods delivered and services rendered. Unreleased appropriations lapse and unexpended funds revert to the Bangsamoro Treasury under a Special Fund for reappropriation under Section 19, Article XII of RA 11054. Only the Chief Minister and the Speaker may declare and use savings, and only to augment actual deficiencies in existing items of their own appropriations. Cash advances may not be granted until earlier ones are liquidated, and an Annual Report on Cash Advances naming the recipients must go to the Committee on Finance, and Budget and Management.

Sections 63–73 (Administrative procedures and final provisions) — Foreign travel of Ministers, Heads of Offices or Agencies and officials at salary grade 25 and above requires clearance from the Office of the Chief Minister. Section 67 requires a status report to the Commission on Audit within 60 days of receiving its Annual Audit Report, published on the agency's website. Section 68 requires financial and physical accountability reports, with failure resulting in “the automatic suspension of the salaries of the responsible official or employee until they have complied”. Section 69 requires publication of each infrastructure project's title, location, description, estimates, winning contractor and bid within 30 calendar days of contract, and of its detailed actual cost and any variation orders within 30 calendar days of the certificate of completion. Section 70 cautions any court, ministry, office or agency against garnishing or subjecting public funds to levy and execution. Section 71 makes payment for the Personnel Services of employees absorbed under Section 10, Article XVI of RA 11054 without prejudice to a funding request to the National Government. Section 73 sets effectivity at 1 January 2024.

who_benefits: Everyone in the region served by Bangsamoro Government programmes
Constituent local government units, whose transfers rise sharply and no longer lapse
Conflict-affected communities, through the ₱5 billion Special Development Fund
Bangsamoro Government personnel, through raised allowances
Women, through the 5% gender and development floor
Communities awaiting infrastructure, with a second year to complete and pay for projects
impact.figures_note: Grand total quoted from Section 1 — a 15.4% increase on FY 2023, the largest year-on-year rise since FY 2021. The Bangsamoro Transition Authority's ₱4,831,206,302 is 4.9% of that total. The Local Government Support Fund is ₱6,536,000,000.00 and the new Share of the Constituent LGUs in Taxes ₱2,033,183,600.00; the Special Development Fund holds at ₱5,000,000,000.00; the Contingent Fund falls to ₱3,775,038,731.00 (3.8% of the budget, against 20.0% in FY 2020). Personnel Services across government are capped at 45% of total revenue sources, at least 5% of every agency budget must go to gender-responsive programmes, and engineering and administrative overhead on infrastructure projects over ₱1,000,000 is capped at 1%.

related_legislation.related_note: This is the first annual budget not followed by an extension act — the 2-year validity in Section 49 removed the need for the sequence that ran BAA 14, BAA 24, BAA 33 and BAA 52. BAA 63, the FY 2024 Supplemental Appropriations Act, added ₱8,441,261,975 in September 2024, funded from previously unspent money. Funding sources and the 45% Personnel Services ceiling derive from Sections 6 and 19 of Article XII of RA 11054, the Organic Law; the ₱5 billion annual Special Development Fund comes from Article XIV of the same law. Remittance of agency income follows Book VII of BAA 13, the Bangsamoro Administrative Code. Section 71 gives effect to Section 10, Article XVI of RA 11054 on absorbed employees. Gender and development follows RA 9710 and reports flow to the Bangsamoro Women Commission created by BAA 8. BAA 84, the Bangsamoro Budget System Act of 2025, later codified as permanent law many of the rules this act carried annually.

implementation_status.irr_status: None required. The finance ministry issues implementing guidelines on cash budgeting, releases, allotment modification and personnel benefits.

implementing_agency.agency: All Bangsamoro ministries, offices and agencies, with the Ministry of Finance, and Budget and Management administering releases

citizen_questions.q: How big was the 2024 regional budget?
citizen_questions.a: ₱98,467,200,000.00, covering 1 January to 31 December 2024 — 15.4% more than the year before, the largest increase since FY 2021. BAA 63 later added ₱8,441,261,975 in supplemental funds.

citizen_questions.q: Where did the money come from?
citizen_questions.a: The annual block grant, other subsidies from the National Government, the region's share of national taxes, fees and charges collected in its territory, unutilized prior years' appropriations from the Bangsamoro Treasury, unutilized prior year's allotments reverted to the Bangsamoro Treasury, and projected collections on regional taxes, fees and charges. The second-to-last of those is new: this budget counts not only unspent appropriations but allotments already issued and given back.

citizen_questions.q: How long was the money available?
citizen_questions.a: Two years. Section 49 made the appropriations available for release and obligation until 31 December 2025 — the first Bangsamoro budget to run beyond a single year — with Personnel Services and General Administration and Support MOOE expiring 31 December 2024. Anything obligated by 31 December 2025 for construction or for goods and services under Support to Operations and Operations stayed “valid until fully expended”.

₱4,831,206,302 through the Bangsamoro Transition Authority — 4.9% of the whole budget. Within its Operations line sit a Legislation programme of ₱1,499,577,140, Representations/Constituency Building at ₱1,654,656,000, Oversight at ₱384,544,000, a Parliamentary Learning Program at ₱40,000,000 and a Philippine Congress–Bangsamoro Parliament Forum at ₱20,000,000.

A Local Government Support Fund of ₱6,536,000,000 — nearly 3 times the FY 2023 figure — plus a new ₱2,033,183,600 line for their share of taxes collected within the region. Under Section 49 neither lapses: both are “available until fully released, obligated, and disbursed”.

Some did. The uniform or clothing allowance rose from ₱6,000 to ₱7,000 a year, and monthly representation and transportation allowances rose for every rank — the Chief Minister from ₱14,000 to ₱15,500, Members of the Parliament from ₱11,000 to ₱12,500, Ministers from ₱9,000 to ₱10,000 and Chiefs of Division from ₱5,000 to ₱6,000. PERA stayed at ₱2,000 a month and the net take-home pay floor stayed at ₱5,000, both unchanged since FY 2020.

citizen_questions.q: What happened to hazard duty pay?
citizen_questions.a: It is not in this act. Every budget from FY 2020 through FY 2023 granted hazard duty pay to personnel in “strife-torn or embattled areas as may be determined and certified by the Secretary of National Defense”. The provision simply does not appear from FY 2024 onward, and the act gives no reason.

citizen_questions.q: Was there a limit on salaries?
citizen_questions.a: Yes. Section 34 caps Personnel Services for one fiscal year at 45% of the Bangsamoro Government's total revenue sources, following Section 6, Article XII of RA 11054.

citizen_questions.q: Could I see proof that a project was built?
citizen_questions.a: Section 69 required agencies to publish each project's title, location, description, cost estimates, winning contractor and bid within 30 calendar days of signing the contract, and the detailed actual cost and any variation orders within 30 calendar days of the certificate of completion.

citizen_questions.q: What happened if an official did not file the required reports?
citizen_questions.a: Section 68 provided for automatic suspension of that official's or employee's salary until they complied, with repeated refusal a ground for administrative disciplinary action.

views.simple: The region's ₱98.47 billion budget for 2024, themed “Accelerating Structural Reforms, Boosting Sustainable Development, and Enhancing Human Capital in the Bangsamoro”. It funds 17 ministries, 11 other executive offices and 6 special purpose funds, and is the first Bangsamoro budget written to run 2 years rather than 1 — ending the practice of passing a separate act each December to extend the expiring budget. Local government transfers rise sharply and stop lapsing altogether. Its 72 sections of operating rules include Personnel Services capped at 45% of revenue, at least 5% of every budget for gender programmes, a 1% ceiling on engineering and administrative overhead, higher representation and clothing allowances, a ₱5,000 net take-home pay floor unchanged since 2020, published contracts and actual costs for every infrastructure project, and automatic salary suspension for officials who fail to report. Hazard duty pay, carried since the first budget, disappears.
